1422.title: Muslim neighbors
1422.hook: the Church esteems Muslims who worship the one God (Nostra Aetate 3)
1422.howItsDone: Catholic teaching on Muslims draws on the Second Vatican Council's declaration Nostra Aetate, which speaks of esteem. Some parishes and dioceses hold meetings, shared meals or service projects with local mosques.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Jewish people, and a pope's name for them. Your line was elder brothers.

Five in the afternoon at a hospital nurses' station. One nurse steps into a supply room, unrolls a small mat, and turns toward the direction she worked out in her first week. Another nurse, a Catholic with a rosary in her scrub pocket, covers the call lights until she's back. Nobody makes a speech. They just know each other's rhythms. A document from the Second Vatican Council, Nostra Aetate, has a short paragraph about exactly this kind of neighbor. Today, Muslim neighbors.
screen: `A MAT IN THE SUPPLY ROOM.` → `A ROSARY IN A SCRUB POCKET.` → `ONE SHORT PARAGRAPH.`

segments.voice: Back on day three hundred twenty-one, this paragraph got a single line. Today, the whole of it. It opens with one word that sets the tone: esteem. The Church regards Muslims with esteem, real regard, more than tolerance or politeness. Then it says why, naming what Muslims actually believe and do, in terms Muslims would recognize. They worship the one God, living, merciful and all-powerful, Creator of heaven and earth, who has spoken to humankind. They strive to submit wholeheartedly to God's decrees, as Abraham did, and Islam gladly links its faith to Abraham. Muslims do not acknowledge Jesus as God, the text says, but they revere him as a prophet. They honor Mary, his virgin mother, and at times call on her with devotion. The council states the difference about Jesus plainly, and still chooses esteem. Muslims await a day of judgment and the raising of the dead. They value the moral life, and worship God especially through prayer, almsgiving and fasting; Catholics keep those same practices in Lent. Finally the council looks back honestly. It admits quarrels and hostilities between Christians and Muslims, and asks both to move past them, to work sincerely for mutual understanding, and together to protect social justice, moral welfare, peace and freedom for everyone. Esteem, then what's shared, then what differs, then a job to do together. It's a short text, and it fits at a nurses' station.

segments.voice: Let one Muslim you actually know, or see often, come to mind: a coworker, a classmate, the family two doors down, the man who runs the corner shop. Recall one thing you know about their day, when they pray or what they care about, hold them with esteem for a moment, and choose a simple greeting for next time; hello, and their name, is plenty. If you pray, you can hold them before God.
Muslim neighbors. In Nostra Aetate the Church regards them with esteem, as worshipers of the one God who pray, give alms and fast. Today's word.
Your line: with esteem. Shared ground and real difference, held side by side. See you tomorrow.

1423.title: Other religions
1423.hook: the Vatican sends greetings for Vesak, Diwali and other feasts
1423.howItsDone: A Vatican office for interreligious dialogue sends messages of greeting for feasts such as Vesak and Diwali, and some Catholic dioceses and parishes join local interfaith gatherings or send greetings to neighboring communities for their feasts.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Muslim neighbors, and the council's careful word for them. Your line was with esteem.

A letter goes out from an office in Rome, addressed to Buddhist friends, for the feast of Vesak. Another goes to Hindu friends, for Diwali, the festival of lights. They come from the Vatican's office for interreligious dialogue, and they read like letters between neighbors: good wishes for the feast, a few lines on something both communities care about, an invitation to work together. Behind them sits one sentence from the Second Vatican Council. Today, other religions.
screen: `A LETTER FOR VESAK.` → `A LETTER FOR DIWALI.` → `ONE SENTENCE BEHIND THEM.`

segments.voice: On day three hundred twenty-one, that sentence was your line: nothing true is rejected. Here it is in full. Nostra Aetate, a little before its paragraph on Muslims, says the Catholic Church rejects nothing that is true and holy in these religions. First it describes other paths in their own terms. Of Hinduism, it says people contemplate the divine mystery, express it through myth and philosophy, and seek release through ascetic practice, deep meditation, and a loving, trusting flight toward God. Of Buddhism, it says it recognizes the insufficiency of this changing world, and teaches a way to reach perfect liberation or supreme illumination. The council isn't grading anyone. It's listening and describing. Then a balancing line, in two halves. The Church looks with sincere respect on ways of acting and teaching that differ from its own, because they often reflect a ray of the truth that enlightens all people. And in the same breath it proclaims Christ, who in John's Gospel says, in the Douay-Rheims, "I am the way, and the truth, and the life." Respect and proclamation sit in one paragraph, not as rivals. Finally, it urges Catholics toward dialogue and collaboration with followers of other religions, with prudence and love, recognizing and promoting the spiritual and moral goods found among them. A letter for Diwali is one small way of doing that. It doesn't say all paths are the same. It says: we see your feast, and we wish you well.
screen: `NOTHING TRUE AND HOLY IS REJECTED.` · `OTHER PATHS DESCRIBED IN THEIR OWN TERMS.` · `RESPECT AND PROCLAMATION, SIDE BY SIDE.` · `DIALOGUE, WITH PRUDENCE AND LOVE.` · then, large: `I AM THE WAY, AND THE TRUTH, AND THE LIFE.`

segments.voice: Let a name come: someone you know who keeps a feast you don't, Diwali, Vesak, Passover, Eid, Vaisakhi, Lunar New Year, whatever is real in your own circle. Shape a greeting for it in plain words, the name of their feast and that you wish them and their family well; nothing more is needed. If you pray, you can hold their household before God.
Other religions. Nostra Aetate says the Church rejects nothing that is true and holy in them, and asks Catholics for dialogue with prudence and love. Today's word.
Your line: greetings of respect. A feast noticed, and a neighbor wished well. Go gently.

1424.title: Seekers
1424.hook: Benedict XVI created a space for dialogue with non-believers
1424.howItsDone: A Vatican office for culture has hosted public gatherings, known as the Courtyard of the Gentiles, where believers and non-believers discuss questions of meaning together. In parishes, some Catholics host open discussion groups or simply spend time listening to friends who do not believe.

segments.voice: Yesterday, other religions, and letters from Rome for Vesak and Diwali. Your line was greetings of respect.

Some families have one person who doesn't fit the usual boxes. Not religious, exactly. Not hostile either. They'll come to midnight Mass at Christmas and stand at the back. They read about the stars late at night and wonder what any of it is for. Ask what they believe and they'll say, honestly, I don't know. Today's neighbor may have no faith at all, and a pope once asked the Church to make room for exactly this person. Today, seekers.
screen: `STANDING AT THE BACK.` → `I DON'T KNOW.` → `A POPE MAKES ROOM.`

segments.voice: Pope Benedict XVI, speaking to the officials who work alongside him in Rome, reached back to the temple in Jerusalem. It had an outer courtyard, he recalled, where people who were not Jews could come close. The Church needs something like that today, he suggested: a place for people to whom God is unknown, and who still don't want to be left simply without God. A place to come close, ask their questions, and be taken seriously. A courtyard, not a debate stage: open air, an open gate, room to walk in and walk out. A Vatican office for culture later took up the name, holding public gatherings where believers and non-believers talked about art, science, meaning and death. Behind the idea are words from the Gospel. In Matthew, Jesus says, in the Douay-Rheims: "Ask, and it shall be given you: seek, and you shall find: knock, and it shall be opened to you." Some readers hear in it a promise for people still looking, not only for those who have arrived. In Acts, in the Athens scene from day five hundred fifty-one, Paul tells the crowd that God made people so that they would seek him, and that he is not far from any one of us. In these texts, seeking is something to honor, not something to fix in one conversation. The question for the courtyard isn't how fast someone gets inside. It's whether they find the gate open, and someone willing to listen.

1425.title: Catholics disagree
1425.hook: the Church holds deep disagreements within one communion
1425.tomorrow: Year four close: the house of many rooms
1425.howItsDone: Catholics share one profession of faith and the same sacraments while holding different views on many open questions, from theology to liturgy to politics. Parishes include people who disagree, and the Church allows different schools of theology and spirituality within its communion.

segments.voice: Yesterday, seekers, and a pope's picture of an open courtyard for people still looking. Your line was the courtyard.

Sunday lunch after Mass. Grandpa misses the Latin. His granddaughter loves the guitar Mass. An uncle reads one Catholic newspaper, an aunt reads another, and they have opinions about each other's. Somebody says the word bishop and the table goes quiet. All of them went to the same Mass that morning, all received communion, and all will be back next week. After days of neighbors of other faiths and none, today's neighbor sits across the table, in the same pew. Catholics disagree.
screen: `SUNDAY LUNCH, AND OPINIONS.` → `THE SAME MASS THAT MORNING.` → `THE NEIGHBOR IN THE SAME PEW.`

segments.voice: Start with the apostles, because they argued too. You met this clash on day six hundred seventy-five, with the two pillars. In Galatians, Paul describes facing Peter at Antioch over eating with Gentile believers, and he doesn't soften it. In the Douay-Rheims: "I withstood him to the face." Two apostles, one Church, a public disagreement, and the New Testament keeps it on the record. The Catechism says that from the beginning the one Church has been marked by great diversity, because God gives many different gifts and the people receiving them differ too. What holds it together: one faith professed, common worship and sacraments, and the succession of bishops from the apostles. Above all, it says, is charity, the bond of perfection. So the Church draws a line. Some things belong to the faith itself, and there it asks for unity. Other questions are left open: how to apply teaching to a hard case, which style of prayer helps, which school of theology makes the most sense. Dominican and Jesuit theologians once argued so hard about how grace works that a pope finally let both schools keep teaching, and told them to stop calling each other heretics. An old Latin saying, which Pope John XXIII quoted, gives the shape: in necessary things unity, in doubtful things liberty, in all things charity. That's one communion up close. Not everyone thinking alike. Everyone at the same altar.
screen: `PAUL WITHSTOOD PETER TO HIS FACE.` · `DIVERSITY FROM THE BEGINNING.` · `ONE FAITH, ONE WORSHIP, ONE BOND OF LOVE.` · `UNITY, LIBERTY, CHARITY.`

segments.voice: Choose one person you disagree with, about church, or politics, or how to raise children, someone you'll actually see this week, and find one thing you genuinely share: a person you both love, a meal you've eaten together, a Mass you've both been to. Hold that, then shape one sentence that names your view without belittling theirs. If you pray, you can ask for patience for you both.
Catholics disagree. From the apostles on, the Church has held real disagreements inside one faith, one worship and one bond of charity. Today's word.
Your line: unity, not sameness. Above every disagreement, charity, the bond of perfection. Until tomorrow.

1426.title: Year four close: the house of many rooms
1426.hook: the Catechism, Aquinas, the orders, justice, Mary and the East: rooms in one house
1426.tomorrow: Year five opens: reading for yourself
1426.howItsDone: Catholics live their faith through different schools of prayer and thought within one Church: some are drawn to a religious order's spirituality, some to social justice, some to Marian devotion or the Eastern liturgies, all sharing the same creed and sacraments.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Catholics disagree, from Paul and Peter at Antioch to Sunday lunch. Your line was unity, not sameness.

A supper table at night, and friends who have just heard their teacher say he is going away. In John's Gospel, Jesus tells them not to let their hearts be troubled, and gives them a picture of a house. In the Douay-Rheims: "In my Father's house there are many mansions." Mansions here means dwelling places, rooms to live in, and the next words speak of a place prepared for them. It's a promise about heaven. It's also a fair picture of this year: a walk through one house, door after door, each room lived in. Today, the year four close.
screen: `SUPPER, THE NIGHT BEFORE.` → `MANY MANSIONS.` → `ONE HOUSE, MANY DOORS.`

segments.voice: On day five hundred eighteen, this verse gave you the line a place for you. Walk back through the house. The first room was the Catechism, read part by part: what Catholics believe, how they celebrate, how they live, and how they pray. That's the floor plan; every other room sits on it. Next, a study, with Thomas Aquinas at the desk, asking a question, listing the objections fairly, answering with patience. Then a long hallway of religious orders. Benedictines, with their rule of prayer and work. Franciscans, with poverty and joy. Dominicans, preaching truth. Jesuits, finding God in all things. Carmelites, climbing into silent prayer. Different rooms for the same Gospel. Then the room that opens onto the street: Catholic social teaching, the dignity of every person, the common good, a preference for the poor. A quieter room with Mary: her feasts, her titles, what the Church teaches about her. A door some Catholics in the West rarely open, into the Eastern Catholic churches, with their own liturgies and icons, in full communion with Rome. And the devotions, the callings and the neighbors: the rosary on a kitchen table, the vocation of a married couple or a hermit, a greeting sent to Muslim, Jewish and Hindu friends. Yesterday, Catholics disagree. Today, where they disagree: inside one house. A Benedictine and a Jesuit pray in different rooms, under one roof, at one table. Not a hotel of strangers. A family home, with doors open between the rooms.

segments.voice: Walk back through the year: the Catechism, Aquinas's study, the orders, social justice, Mary, the East, the devotions and the callings.
